verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster: 'Al-tashchet' [Do not destroy]. A psalm of Asaph, a song.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the one who leads the singing. Set to the tune that begins, Do not destroy. A psalm of Asaph. A song.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the heading, and in the Hebrew Bible it is the first verse of the psalm, which the KJV prints unnumbered. Treat it as the stage direction. 'Choirmaster' is a temple office: the leader of a Levitical guild whose name here is Asaph, a family of singers and not a single poet. 'Al-tashchet' is most likely the name of a melody or a setting, as in Psalms 57-59, where the same words stand in the heading. Meiri links the phrase to David's 'Do not destroy him' to Abishai (1 Samuel 26:9). The KJV leaves it as a transliteration, which is honest; the words mean 'Do not destroy', and the audience would have heard a plea against ruin before the first line is sung. Rashi hears it as God being asked not to destroy Israel. Keep the plea light and in the background: it colours the whole psalm, which ends with a promise that judgment is real but measured.

philological_notes.note: 'Do not destroy': a negative command from sh-ch-t, 'to ruin, corrupt, destroy'. As a heading it is probably the name of a tune (so also Psalms 57, 58, 59). The commentators read it as a prayer, and the sense of the words is a plea against ruin.
'To the leader/choirmaster': a participle from n-tz-ch, the verb meaning to excel, to oversee. The KJV 'chief Musician' is sound; the word names the person responsible for the performance.

verses.translation_literal: We give thanks to you, O God; we give thanks, and near [is] your name; they recount your wonders.
verses.translation_dramatic: We give thanks to you, O God. We give thanks, and the sound of it carries, for your name is near. Your wonders are told, and told again.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm opens in a crowd. 'We give thanks' is said twice, and the repetition is the point: it is liturgy, a thing said together and more than once, and it should be sung loudly enough that a stranger could hear it. The second clause is the one translators fight over. 'Your name is near' means that God has made himself present and reachable, and the next clause, 'they recount your wonders', says how: the wonders are told over by people who saw them or heard of them. The KJV runs the two together into 'thy name is near thy wondrous works declare', which reads like a printing error. It makes 'thy wondrous works' the subject of 'declare', as if the wonders themselves did the telling. The Hebrew has an unnamed 'they' who recount, with 'your wonders' as the thing recounted. Ibn Ezra takes the 'they' to be the prophets, Metzudat David the fathers, and Malbim hears the wonders as proof that the name is near. The KJV also turns the plain 'and' into 'for that'. The 'name' is more than a label in this world: it is the presence and reputation of the one named, as in 'the name of the LORD' in the temple.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of y-d-h, 'to give thanks, to confess, to praise'. The root also means to acknowledge publicly, so the verse is an open declaration, not a private feeling. It is repeated for emphasis (Radak: 'the doubling strengthens the thanks').

Piel perfect, third person plural, 'they recounted, they told'. The subject is unnamed: Ibn Ezra says the prophets, Metzudat David the fathers. 'Your wonders' is its object, not its subject as in the KJV.

'And near is your name': an adjective and a noun with no verb. The KJV 'for that thy name is near' supplies a 'for' that the Hebrew lacks; the clause is joined by a simple 'and'. Malbim reads it as the wonders proving that the name is near.

verses.translation_literal: For I will take an appointed time; I, I will judge uprightness.
verses.translation_dramatic: I will choose the hour. I myself will judge, and I will judge straight.
verses.directors_commentary: A new voice breaks in, and in the line's logic it is God's: he is the one who sets the date. Play it quiet and slow, because the speaker is in no hurry, and the delay is the reason for the speech. 'I will take' (the verb is 'take', not 'receive') means that he chooses and grasps the moment; it is his, not the court's. The KJV 'when I shall receive the congregation' is a mistranslation: mo'ed is a fixed, appointed time (the word for the festivals, and the 'tent of meeting' is its cousin), and the plain sense is 'when the time comes that I have set'. 'Judge uprightness' is a plural abstract, 'straightnesses', used as an adverb: I will judge fairly. The pronoun 'I' is doubled, which is the emphasis the KJV drops. The idea behind the line is the ancient Near Eastern king who holds court on a fixed day: the oppressed wait for it, and the powerful are afraid of it. Rashi reads the whole line differently, as the people at a festival giving their attention to praise; the plain sense does not need that.

philological_notes.note: 'Appointed time': from y-'-d, 'to appoint, to meet'. The same word names the festivals and the 'tent of meeting'. In this line it is the time God has fixed for judgment. The KJV 'congregation' picks up the sense of an assembly, which this word has elsewhere but does not carry here.
A plural of intensity, 'straightness, equity': what is level and not crooked. Used elsewhere of fair judgment (Ps 9:9, 96:10).

verses.translation_literal: Melting [are] the earth and all its inhabitants; I, I have regulated its pillars. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: The earth is melting, and everything that lives on it, running like wax before a fire. But I am the one who set its pillars true, and they stand. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the verse that tells the actors how big the stage is. The earth is imagined as a building on pillars, the ancient Near Eastern picture of the world (see also 1 Samuel 2:8, Job 9:6, Psalm 104:5), and when the world 'melts' it is as if it were wax or snow. The verb is the one used for people losing heart in terror (Joshua 2:9) and for hills melting before God, so this is a picture of a world going soft with fear, and the speaker's steady hand is set against it. The KJV 'I bear up the pillars' makes God an Atlas carrying the load: the Hebrew verb is about measuring and regulating, not carrying, and 'I have set them in order' is closer. The doubled 'I' returns, a flat, calm claim. 'Selah' is a musical marker of uncertain meaning, probably a pause or a rise. Mark it in the script as a held beat.

philological_notes.note: 'Melting, dissolving': from m-w-g, used of hearts or peoples losing courage (Josh 2:9, 24) and of the earth quaking (Amos 9:5). The plural participle agrees with 'earth and all its inhabitants' taken together.

From t-k-n, 'to measure, to weigh, to regulate'. It is used elsewhere of God weighing the spirits (Prov 16:2) and measuring the waters (Isa 40:12). The KJV 'bear up' guesses from context; 'I have regulated, set in order' is the lexical sense.
A liturgical marker of unknown meaning, probably a pause, a musical interlude or a lifting of voices. It is left untranslated.

verses.translation_literal: I said to the boasters, 'Do not boast,' and to the wicked, 'Do not lift up a horn.'
verses.translation_dramatic: I have said it to the braggarts: stop your bragging. I have said it to the wicked: do not raise your horn.
verses.directors_commentary: The speaker turns to the crowd of the proud, and the voice hardens. The Hebrew plays on one root: 'to the boasters (holelim) do not boast (tahollu)', and a good delivery repeats the sound like a slap. English 'deal not foolishly' (KJV) loses it, and has also softened it, because the root h-l-l here means loud, reckless self-praise, not foolishness in general. 'Horn' is the image of strength in a world of cattle and wild oxen: the beast with its head up and its horns raised is dangerous, and in Hebrew poetry the lifted horn is a boast of power (1 Samuel 2:1, Psalm 92:10). The KJV keeps 'horn', which is right, but a modern audience hears only the animal, so make the gesture visible: the chin lifts. The verb 'I said' is a perfect, not a threat in the future: it is something already warned, and the ruin to come is the result of not listening.

philological_notes.note: A participle and a verb of the same root h-l-l (II), 'to be boastful, to act madly'. Not the same h-l-l as 'praise', but the sound play is deliberate. The KJV 'fools... deal not foolishly' keeps the pairing but dilutes it.
'Horn': a symbol of strength and pride (1 Sam 2:1, Ps 89:18). To lift the horn is to boast, and to cut it off (v. 11) is to humble.

verses.translation_literal: Do not lift up your horn to the height; do not speak with a neck of arrogance.
verses.translation_dramatic: Do not raise your horn against the heights. Do not speak with your neck thrown back and your words grown huge.
verses.directors_commentary: The warning is repeated, and the second half gives the image a body. 'To the height' (la-marom) is the sky, which is God's place: the boast is not just louder than others but pointed upward, at heaven. 'Speak with a neck' is an odd phrase and the KJV flattens it to 'a stiff neck', which brings in the separate idiom of 'stiff-necked' (qeshe 'oref) for stubborn Israel; the Hebrew has tzavvar 'atak, a neck of 'atak, 'arrogance' or 'hardness', and the picture is an actor's: head back, throat out, a thick neck of a man full of himself, talking up at the sky. Radak adds that the thick neck is a fat, well-fed one, so that the boasts come from comfort. Direct the speaker to stretch, not to stiffen. The word 'atak (later 'insolence, defiance') is the same word used of 'hard things' spoken against God in Psalm 31:19 and 94:4.

philological_notes.note: 'With a neck of arrogance': 'atak is an adjective, 'hard, bold, arrogant', and describes either the neck or the speech. Ibn Ezra offers both; Radak reads a thick, fat neck. Not the same as 'stiff-necked' (qeshe 'oref).

verses.translation_literal: For [it is] not from the going out and from the setting, and not from the wilderness [is] lifting up.
verses.translation_dramatic: For no lifting comes from the sunrise, nor from the sunset, nor from the wilderness. Not from any of these will anyone be raised.
verses.directors_commentary: The sentence has no verb, as if the speaker were so impatient that the sentence breaks off. The points of the compass are 'the going out' (where the sun comes out) and 'the setting': east and west. The KJV adds 'nor from the south', and the third phrase, 'mimmidbar harim', is the reason. It can be read 'from the wilderness of mountains', and the Targum takes it that way, as the southern desert, the place of the mountains; the KJV's 'south' follows the Targum. Or it can be read 'from the wilderness [is] lifting up', with harim a noun from the same root as the verb 'lift' in vv. 5, 6 and 8. Radak and Meiri take the second, and argue from the vowel under the bet of mimmidbar: in their text it is a qamets, so the word is not in the construct and cannot govern harim. Our text points it with a patah, the construct, so that argument does not carry here, but the sense still suits the psalm: promotion comes from no direction, east, west or desert, and the next verse gives the answer: it comes from God, who lifts up. The KJV's 'promotion' is a good rendering of the idea. The audience would have thought of trade caravans and conquests, the routes by which a man rose in the world.

philological_notes.note: Either 'from the wilderness of mountains' (har, plural harim, read by the Targum as the southern desert, and followed by KJV 'south') or 'from the wilderness [is] lifting up' (harim from r-w-m, 'to lift'). Radak and Meiri support the second by the qamets 'under the bet' in their text, which would make midbar not construct; our text has patah (construct), so the reading rests on the sense and the echo of vv. 5-8.

'Going out' (of the sun) and 'setting place' (of the sun): the ordinary Hebrew names for east and west. Rashi glosses them as the sun's rising and setting. Meiri reads the three terms as lineage, wealth and wisdom, which is his own gloss.

token_glosses.gloss: from the going out [of the sun]

verses.translation_literal: For God [is] judge; this one he brings low, and this one he lifts up.
verses.translation_dramatic: For it is God who judges. This one he brings low, and that one he lifts up.
verses.directors_commentary: Here is the answer the last verse was waiting for, and it is short. 'God is judge' has no 'the' in the Hebrew: it is a statement of who he is, 'a judge', in the same way you say 'he is king'. The line is a hinge, because the verb 'lift up' (hérim) comes back from vv. 5-7: the proud 'lifted' their own horns, and now the one who lifts is the only one with the right. The pointing gesture helps: 'this one', 'this one', two fingers, two men. The KJV 'putteth down... setteth up' is a good, old-fashioned rendering, but 'lift' is the verb the whole psalm has been repeating, so keep the echo. The reversal of rich and poor is a theme found in Hannah's song (1 Samuel 2:7) and the later Magnificat, where the powerful are brought down and the humble lifted.

philological_notes.note: Two hiphil verbs, 'bring low' and 'lift up', set against each other. 'Lift up' repeats the verb of vv. 5-6 (taRimu), so God's judgment is described with the same verb as the boasters' crime.

verses.translation_literal: For a cup [is] in the hand of YHWH, and wine foams, full of spice; and he pours out from this; surely its dregs they will drain, they will drink, all the wicked of the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: For there is a cup in the hand of the LORD, and the wine in it foams, thick with spice. He tips it, and it pours. And the dregs, the very bottom of it, they will drain to the last drop, they will drink it down, every wicked one on the earth.
verses.directors_commentary: The image is a banquet, and the audience knew what kind. In the ancient Near East wine was drunk mixed, with water or, as here, with spices, and the foaming, fermenting wine of this cup is as strong as it can be. The 'cup in the hand of the LORD' is the cup of his wrath (Isaiah 51:17, Jeremiah 25:15, Psalm 11:6): drunk, it makes a man stagger. Rashi calls it the cup of reeling (tar'elah), and the Targum adds bitterness to the mixture. The host holds it himself; the scene is domestic and terrible, a host who does not leave the table. The KJV renders chamar 'red', which is Radak's Arabic gloss; the Hebrew verb means 'to foam, to ferment'. 'It is full of mixture' is correct but hard to hear, so the spiced drink is the point. For yimtzu the KJV has 'wring them out'. The root m-ts-h has both senses, 'drain, suck out' (Metzudat Zion) and 'wring out' (the fleece of Judges 6:38); 'wring out' is therefore possible, but 'drain' fits drinking dregs better, and the picture is of men forced to the dregs, which in a wine jar lie thick at the bottom. The verb 'pours' is the one used of water poured down a slope (Micah 1:4), a long steady stream. Play the pour slowly.

philological_notes.note: 'Cup': in the prophets, the cup of God's wrath or judgment, whose contents make a drinker reel (Isa 51:17, Jer 25:15, Ps 11:6). Rashi names it the cup of reeling (tar'elah); the Targum has a mixture of bitterness. Here the only cup is in God's own hand.
A verb, 'it foams, it ferments' (cf. Ps 46:4, of waters). The KJV 'red' follows the Arabic ahmar via Radak; foaming wine is the more common sense.
'Mixture, spiced wine': from m-s-kh, 'to mix'. Wine mixed with spices or water (Prov 9:2, 5). The word marks a strong, rich drink.

'They will drain': Metzudat Zion derives it from mitzitzah, 'sucking', so to drain or suck out. The same root means 'wring out' in Judges 6:38, which is the KJV and YLT rendering. Both are attested; 'drain' suits dregs better.
'Its dregs': the sediment that settles at the bottom of a wine jar (Isa 25:6, Jer 48:11). The wicked get what the host leaves for last.

verses.translation_literal: And I, I will declare for ever; I will sing praise to the God of Jacob.
verses.translation_dramatic: But I will tell of it for ever. I will sing to the God of Jacob.
verses.directors_commentary: The cup is put down and the singer steps forward. The 'I' of this verse stands against the 'wicked' of the last one, and it is a human voice, the psalmist's, though Radak and Meiri hear Israel as a whole. The sentence begins with 'and I', the word that turns the scene: the proud had their boast, and this is the answer, a vow of endless praise. 'Declare' (aggid) is the verb of reporting news, and 'sing praise' (azammerah) is the verb of music with an instrument, so the voice should go from speech to song within the line. 'God of Jacob' is the old covenant title, the God of the ancestor who struggled and was lifted, an apt close to a psalm about reversal. The KJV 'for ever' is right (le'olam is 'to the distant time'); BBE's 'full of joy' is a paraphrase of 'declare' that the text does not support.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of n-g-d, 'to make known, to report, to declare', normally of telling news or facts. The object, the judgment and wonders just described, is left unstated.
'I will sing praise', with the cohortative ending -ah, a self-exhortation ('let me sing'). The root z-m-r is the one that gives mizmor, 'psalm', in the heading (v. 1).

verses.translation_literal: And all the horns of the wicked I will cut off; the horns of the righteous will be lifted up.
verses.translation_dramatic: And every horn of the wicked I will cut down. But the horns of the righteous shall be raised high.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm ends where it began, with the horn, and the image is now complete. The proud lifted their horns (vv. 5-6); here the horns of the wicked are cut off. The verb 'cut off' (gada') is used of felling trees (Isaiah 9:9) and cutting bars (Psalm 107:16), so it is a blunt, physical word, as if to saw off the horns of a bull. Against it stands 'will be lifted up', the same verb as before, in a feminine plural that agrees with 'horns': what the wicked try to do for themselves is done, in the end, for the righteous. Who says 'I will cut off' is disputed, and the director must choose. Radak and Metzudat David hear Israel, the 'I' of v. 10, cutting off the horns with God's strength: Radak places it in the wars of Gog and Magog, and Metzudat David has God give strength into the speaker's hand. Rashi too has Israel cut off the horn of Amalek (Ezekiel 25:14). The other reading takes God as the speaker, continuing the voice of vv. 3-4 and the judge of v. 8; it is the more natural flow of the Hebrew, which has no quotation marks, but it is a reading and the commentators here do not state it. Either way the line is a promise that the lifted horn belongs to God to give. The KJV 'also' is a loose rendering of the plain 'and'. 'Righteous' is a singular, 'the righteous one', used as a class, while 'horns' is plural. Bring the chapter down in a plain, held ending.

philological_notes.note: 'I will cut off', a piel of g-d-', 'to hew, to chop down' (Metzudat Zion compares Isa 9:9). Used for cutting down trees and for breaking horns (Lam 2:3). Rashi connects this verse to Ezekiel 25:14, where Israel is the agent. The identity of the 'I' is disputed: see the reviewer note.

'They will be lifted up': a polel-type stem of r-w-m with the feminine plural ending -nah, agreeing with 'horns'. Meiri notes that it is an intransitive verb. It echoes taRimu and yaRim in vv. 5-8, so the psalm ends on its key word.
